medical.title: Routine breast imaging may offer little benefit after double mastectomy for early breast cancer
medical.summary: Women who have undergone a double mastectomy to treat ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), a noninvasive form of breast cancer also known as stage 0 breast cancer, may not benefit from routine mammograms or other breast imaging after surgery, according to a new study led by investigators at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center.

medical.title: Replacing dairy products with unfortified plant-based alternatives could lead to deficiencies in certain nutrients
medical.summary: Replacing dairy products, even partially, with unfortified plant-based alternatives may lead to a deficiency in vital nutrients, a new study from the University of Surrey reports. Mandatory fortification of plant-based alternatives and other foods, including bread, could lessen the risk of deficiencies, particularly iodine deficiency.

medical.title: How a CRISPR sickle cell therapy moved from lab to clinical trial
medical.summary: A UCLA-led team has described how it advanced an experimental CRISPR approach for sickle cell disease into a blood stem cell therapy that can be manufactured at the scale and quality required for a clinical trial.

medical.title: Why humans are more sensitive than other species to a brain developmental disease
medical.summary: Researchers at VIB and KU Leuven have uncovered how mutations in the ASPM gene disrupt the development of neural stem cells that help the human brain grow. This disruption explains how these mutations cause microcephaly, a condition characterized by an abnormally small brain and head, often accompanied by intellectual disability. The discovery, published in Developmental Cell, also sheds light on how differences in brain development can make humans more susceptible to certain genetic conditions than other mammals.

medical.title: From DNA marks to RNA control: A new clue to acute myeloid leukemia
medical.summary: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is an aggressive blood cancer in which abnormal, immature cells build up in the bone marrow, disrupting the production of healthy blood cells. Now, a new study, led by Dr. José Luis Sardina's group at the Josep Carreras Leukaemia Research Institute (IJC), examines how two systems that help control normal blood cell development are connected: the chemical marks on DNA and the regulation of RNA, which carries instructions for making proteins. The work is published in the journal Science Advances.

medical.title: Tiny structures in our spines could hold clues to why our backs wear out
medical.summary: An international team of scientists has discovered how some of the tiniest structures in the human spine help it cope with the strain of bending, lifting and everyday movement, potentially shedding new light on why spinal disks deteriorate.

medical.title: Chronic illness linked to higher prescription drug misuse
medical.summary: Working-age adults who manage more chronic health conditions are more likely to misuse prescription medications, researchers in the Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs found.

medical.title: Protein DUSP4 boosts cancer-fighting T cells in colorectal cancer lab models
medical.summary: The immune system has powerful cells that can recognize and destroy cancer, but this ability can gradually wane when the cells reside within a tumor. Researchers from the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (NUS Medicine), and their collaborators have identified a protein that could help keep these cancer-fighting immune cells active and potentially provide a new way to strengthen engineered T-cell therapies against colorectal cancer.

medical.title: Generative AI fills gaps in brain wiring maps where MRI scans lose signal
medical.summary: Researchers from the Mark and Mary Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute (Stevens INI) at the Keck School of Medicine of USC have developed an artificial intelligence (AI) model that helps fill gaps in brain wiring maps made with diffusion MRI, a type of scan that traces the brain's nerve fiber pathways. This could help researchers study how key brain connections change with aging and disease.

medical.title: Exposure to petroleum-based lubricants at work associated with multiple sclerosis risk
medical.summary: Exposure to petroleum-derived lubricants at work, including engine oil, hydraulic oil and cutting fluids used to cool or lubricate metal during metalworking, is associated with higher odds of multiple sclerosis (MS), according to a study published in Neurology. The study does not prove that exposure to these lubricants causes MS. It only shows an association.

medical.title: Longer estrogen exposure linked to better brain vessel health in older women
medical.summary: Women who had a longer reproductive period and had used or are using hormone replacement therapy showed fewer signs of damage to the small blood vessels in the brain later in life. This is shown by a study led by researchers at Karolinska Institutet, published in the journal Neurology.

medical.title: Blood pressure medication and vibration may boost brain waste clearance
medical.summary: The brain's own clearance mechanisms are most active during sleep. Researchers have now shown that this natural clearance process can also be enhanced while people are awake. A novel vasomechanical treatment increased the removal of harmful proteins from participants' brains.

medical.title: AI starts writing acne prescriptions without a doctor's visit in one state
medical.summary: Utah has become the first state to let an artificial intelligence (AI) program prescribe medication without a doctor writing the prescription, starting with acne treatments.

medical.title: New CRISPR proteins expand editing access to heart disease genes
medical.summary: Rice University's Han Xiao has used his AI-supported Sequence Display technology to expand the targeting abilities of CRISPR/Cas9. In a paper recently published in Nature Communications, Xiao evolved several variants of a compact Cas9 that could efficiently target stretches of DNA previously inaccessible for editing. The research included a proof-of-concept study in which the evolved Cas9s were successfully used to edit two genes found in coronary heart disease.

medical.title: Key gene preserves lifelong supply of stem cells that make bone healing possible, study suggests
medical.summary: The action of a key gene is required to maintain a lifelong supply of stem cells that make bone healing possible, a new study finds.

medical.title: Rapid tau spread may explain why midlife Alzheimer's progresses more rapidly
medical.summary: Patients with early-onset Alzheimer's disease, whose symptoms start before age 65, have more extensive deposits of tau, a hallmark protein of the condition, compared with patients whose symptoms start at 65-plus, a new study found. What's more, tau accumulates at more than twice the rate in younger compared to older patients and spreads widely throughout the brain.

medical.title: Experimental ultrasound implant could help guide care after spinal cord injury
medical.summary: A team of engineers and surgeons from Johns Hopkins Medicine has published its first proof-of-concept study that shows temporarily implanting a tiny ultrasonic device into the location of a spinal cord injury can be feasible, safe and potentially useful. These findings, which mark an early midpoint in a multitiered research journey to develop and study how the device could be used in clinical care, were published in Science Advances.

medical.title: From green smoothies to stem‑cell supplements—online 'immune‑boosting' ideas may lead you astray
medical.summary: We all want a well-functioning immune system to help us fight invasive bacteria and viruses and recover faster from illness. Popular "immune-boosting" ideas, however, might be more of a hindrance than a help.

science.summary: The third-largest island in the Mediterranean Sea exposes an ancient piece of the ocean floor and hosts a clowder of cats.

science.title: Why so many British pubs are closing down
science.summary: British pubs are disappearing at an alarming rate. Last year, around eight closed down every week.

This high-performance, highly adaptable research platform is designed to accelerate the development and testing of advanced aviation technologies.  The crewed X-70 features advanced, rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology that will allow NASA to explore […]

science.title: Japan's ALS community is ready to become research partners, nationwide survey suggests
science.summary: People living with ALS and their families in Japan are eager to help shape research on the disease, even though most have never heard of patient and public involvement (PPI), according to a study published on Oct. 30, 2026, in Research Involvement and Engagement.

science.title: A new route to calculating gluon production in proton–nucleus collisions
science.summary: In the theoretical study of proton-nucleus collisions, the colliding projectiles can be described as streams of color charges moving along their respective trajectories. These color charges couple to gluons, which then produce the particles that are observed in the final state (gluons and quarks, which eventually produce hadrons).

science.title: Earth atmosphere emulators could enable faster and more accurate weather predictions
science.summary: If you partitioned the entire Earth, from just below the surface to the top of the atmosphere, into 1-kilometer-square chunks, there would be billions of them. Now run each of those cells through a series of complex physics equations, and you can see how the entire Earth system interacts and evolves in detail, one step at a time.

science.title: How ranchers on Brazil's 'Dirty List' bypass forced labor safeguards by selling cattle through intermediaries
science.summary: Brazil's "Dirty List," a public registry that names employers found to have violated anti-slavery laws, is a key component of the country's efforts to combat forced labor. Major meatpackers in Brazil signed sustainable sourcing commitments promising to not purchase cattle directly from ranchers on the Dirty List. But new research shows that ranchers have found ways around these restrictions, rerouting cattle through intermediaries and allowing cattle linked to forced labor to remain in domestic and international beef and leather supply chains.

science.title: First direct observations reveal hydrogen dissolved in tiny gaps between metal atoms
science.summary: University of Sydney researchers have made a breakthrough by directly observing hydrogen in the tiny spaces between the atoms in metal alloys. The world-first observation of hydrogen dissolving in these 'metal crystal lattices' offers fresh insights into why hydrogen can weaken metals and how more hydrogen-resistant materials might be developed.

science.title: Scientists reveal how cosignaling receptors dually regulate T cell activation via phase separation
science.summary: Previous studies have shown that upon antigen stimulation, the T cell receptor (TCR) undergoes phase separation with the kinase Lck to mediate rapid T cell activation. However, the manner in which costimulating receptors regulate this process has remained unclear.

environment.title: Suriname’s rich archaeological history may hold keys to conservation
environment.summary: Suriname pledges to save its forests but neglects the ancient human history hidden within them, experts say.

environment.title: A town-wide ‘living laboratory’ shows how green spaces can combat climate extremes
environment.summary: Stoke Park is a natural haven in a busy British town. Centered in Guildford, Surrey, its rolling fields pop with wildflowers in the spring; birds sing and ducks paddle serenely in a pond beside ornamental gardens; and the sun casts dappled shade on the grass from oak, spruce and beech trees, scattered across 52 hectares […]

environment.title: Why I sent my archive of nature’s sounds to France (commentary)
environment.summary: It is a peculiar irony: as technology reaches ever deeper into Earth’s living systems, the primal sonic expressions of the natural world—wind, water, leaf, and creature—have never been more imperiled. Soundscape ecology rests on a simple conviction: the collective voices of the nonhuman world are not only eloquent, but essential. Recorded and preserved over time, […]

environment.title: US public lands tracker highlights the collective impact of Trump policies
environment.summary: In his second term as the U.S. president, Donald Trump has taken actions to remove protections from at least 34.8 million hectares (86 million acres) of public lands, according to the advocacy group Center for American Progress. The nonprofit Conservation Lands Foundation (CLF) recently catalogued 12 such policy actions in its newly released Public Lands […]

environment.title: Cyclone batters India’s eastern coast, killing 3 and damaging homes and farmland
environment.summary: KAKINADA, India (AP) — A powerful cyclone battered India ’s Andhra Pradesh state on Wednesday, killing at least three people and damaging homes and farmland after authorities evacuated tens of thousands of people, officials said. Cyclone Arnab made landfall early Wednesday as a very severe cyclonic storm before weakening to a severe cyclonic storm as […]

environment.title: Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has vanished in just five years
environment.summary: Switzerland’s glaciers are disappearing at an alarming rate, losing more than 5% of their ice volume in 2026 alone. Some of the country’s most famous glaciers experienced their worst melting on record, while several smaller glaciers vanished completely. Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has disappeared in just five years, driven by unusually snowless winters and extreme summer heat.

environment.title: Scientists discover a surprising twist in Japan's 7,300-year-old volcanic apocalypse
environment.summary: A catastrophic volcanic eruption 7,300 years ago devastated Japan, but new research reveals that its impact on prehistoric populations was far more complex than previously believed. While some communities disappeared or declined, others unexpectedly flourished as survivors migrated, adapted, and found new ways to thrive.

environment.title: DNA recording system reveals how a single cell becomes a body
environment.summary: Scientists have traced the development of a mouse embryo from its first two cells to the formation of organs, using a remarkable DNA recording system that reveals the family history of individual cells. Their findings uncover how different cell types emerge on their own schedules and could help explain what goes wrong in birth defects, genetic disorders, and cancer.

environment.title: Europe's new Sentinel-3C satellite just sent back spectacular images of Earth
environment.summary: Europe's Sentinel-3C satellite has returned breathtaking images of Earth just two weeks after launch, revealing the snowy Alps, frozen Arctic islands, and brilliant turquoise Caribbean waters. Its first measurements also show promising results for tracking rising seas, melting ice sheets, and other changes reshaping our planet.

environment.title: Scientists uncover the 2.3-billion-year-old secret that helped keep Earth habitable
environment.summary: Scientists may have solved a 2.3-billion-year-old mystery about how Earth maintained enough oxygen to support life. Ancient rocks reveal that phosphorus recycling in the oceans created a self-sustaining cycle that helped keep oxygen levels high, even as the planet underwent dramatic environmental changes. The discovery challenges assumptions about Earth's early atmosphere and raises new questions about why complex life took so long to emerge.

environment.title: Scientists find a surprising genetic twist behind octopus intelligence
environment.summary: The remarkable intelligence of octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish may trace back to an ancient reshuffling of their DNA that created new connections between genes. Scientists discovered that these changes in the genome's 3D structure may have helped drive the evolution of their unusually complex nervous systems.

mix_items.title: Cyprus: Island of Snakes, Cats, and Ophiolites
mix_items.summary: The third-largest island in the Mediterranean Sea exposes an ancient piece of the ocean floor and hosts a clowder of cats.

mix_items.title: Why so many British pubs are closing down
mix_items.summary: British pubs are disappearing at an alarming rate. Last year, around eight closed down every week.

mix_items.title: NASA Announces X-70 Experimental Aircraft to Advance Flight Research
mix_items.summary: On Wednesday, NASA unveiled its newest experimental aircraft, the X-70 Fractal, during the UP.Summit at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. This high-performance, highly adaptable research platform is designed to accelerate the development and testing of advanced aviation technologies.  The crewed X-70 features advanced, rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology that will allow NASA to explore […]

mix_items.title: Japan's ALS community is ready to become research partners, nationwide survey suggests
mix_items.summary: People living with ALS and their families in Japan are eager to help shape research on the disease, even though most have never heard of patient and public involvement (PPI), according to a study published on Oct. 30, 2026, in Research Involvement and Engagement.

mix_items.title: A new route to calculating gluon production in proton–nucleus collisions
mix_items.summary: In the theoretical study of proton-nucleus collisions, the colliding projectiles can be described as streams of color charges moving along their respective trajectories. These color charges couple to gluons, which then produce the particles that are observed in the final state (gluons and quarks, which eventually produce hadrons).

mix_items.title: Earth atmosphere emulators could enable faster and more accurate weather predictions
mix_items.summary: If you partitioned the entire Earth, from just below the surface to the top of the atmosphere, into 1-kilometer-square chunks, there would be billions of them. Now run each of those cells through a series of complex physics equations, and you can see how the entire Earth system interacts and evolves in detail, one step at a time.

mix_items.title: How ranchers on Brazil's 'Dirty List' bypass forced labor safeguards by selling cattle through intermediaries
mix_items.summary: Brazil's "Dirty List," a public registry that names employers found to have violated anti-slavery laws, is a key component of the country's efforts to combat forced labor. Major meatpackers in Brazil signed sustainable sourcing commitments promising to not purchase cattle directly from ranchers on the Dirty List. But new research shows that ranchers have found ways around these restrictions, rerouting cattle through intermediaries and allowing cattle linked to forced labor to remain in domestic and international beef and leather supply chains.

mix_items.title: First direct observations reveal hydrogen dissolved in tiny gaps between metal atoms
mix_items.summary: University of Sydney researchers have made a breakthrough by directly observing hydrogen in the tiny spaces between the atoms in metal alloys. The world-first observation of hydrogen dissolving in these 'metal crystal lattices' offers fresh insights into why hydrogen can weaken metals and how more hydrogen-resistant materials might be developed.

mix_items.title: Scientists reveal how cosignaling receptors dually regulate T cell activation via phase separation
mix_items.summary: Previous studies have shown that upon antigen stimulation, the T cell receptor (TCR) undergoes phase separation with the kinase Lck to mediate rapid T cell activation. However, the manner in which costimulating receptors regulate this process has remained unclear.

mix_items.title: Routine breast imaging may offer little benefit after double mastectomy for early breast cancer
mix_items.summary: Women who have undergone a double mastectomy to treat ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), a noninvasive form of breast cancer also known as stage 0 breast cancer, may not benefit from routine mammograms or other breast imaging after surgery, according to a new study led by investigators at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center.

mix_items.title: Replacing dairy products with unfortified plant-based alternatives could lead to deficiencies in certain nutrients
mix_items.summary: Replacing dairy products, even partially, with unfortified plant-based alternatives may lead to a deficiency in vital nutrients, a new study from the University of Surrey reports. Mandatory fortification of plant-based alternatives and other foods, including bread, could lessen the risk of deficiencies, particularly iodine deficiency.

mix_items.title: How a CRISPR sickle cell therapy moved from lab to clinical trial
mix_items.summary: A UCLA-led team has described how it advanced an experimental CRISPR approach for sickle cell disease into a blood stem cell therapy that can be manufactured at the scale and quality required for a clinical trial.

mix_items.title: Why humans are more sensitive than other species to a brain developmental disease
mix_items.summary: Researchers at VIB and KU Leuven have uncovered how mutations in the ASPM gene disrupt the development of neural stem cells that help the human brain grow. This disruption explains how these mutations cause microcephaly, a condition characterized by an abnormally small brain and head, often accompanied by intellectual disability. The discovery, published in Developmental Cell, also sheds light on how differences in brain development can make humans more susceptible to certain genetic conditions than other mammals.

mix_items.title: From DNA marks to RNA control: A new clue to acute myeloid leukemia
mix_items.summary: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is an aggressive blood cancer in which abnormal, immature cells build up in the bone marrow, disrupting the production of healthy blood cells. Now, a new study, led by Dr. José Luis Sardina's group at the Josep Carreras Leukaemia Research Institute (IJC), examines how two systems that help control normal blood cell development are connected: the chemical marks on DNA and the regulation of RNA, which carries instructions for making proteins. The work is published in the journal Science Advances.

mix_items.title: Tiny structures in our spines could hold clues to why our backs wear out
mix_items.summary: An international team of scientists has discovered how some of the tiniest structures in the human spine help it cope with the strain of bending, lifting and everyday movement, potentially shedding new light on why spinal disks deteriorate.

mix_items.title: Chronic illness linked to higher prescription drug misuse
mix_items.summary: Working-age adults who manage more chronic health conditions are more likely to misuse prescription medications, researchers in the Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs found.

mix_items.title: Protein DUSP4 boosts cancer-fighting T cells in colorectal cancer lab models
mix_items.summary: The immune system has powerful cells that can recognize and destroy cancer, but this ability can gradually wane when the cells reside within a tumor. Researchers from the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (NUS Medicine), and their collaborators have identified a protein that could help keep these cancer-fighting immune cells active and potentially provide a new way to strengthen engineered T-cell therapies against colorectal cancer.

mix_items.title: Generative AI fills gaps in brain wiring maps where MRI scans lose signal
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the Mark and Mary Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute (Stevens INI) at the Keck School of Medicine of USC have developed an artificial intelligence (AI) model that helps fill gaps in brain wiring maps made with diffusion MRI, a type of scan that traces the brain's nerve fiber pathways. This could help researchers study how key brain connections change with aging and disease.

mix_items.title: Exposure to petroleum-based lubricants at work associated with multiple sclerosis risk
mix_items.summary: Exposure to petroleum-derived lubricants at work, including engine oil, hydraulic oil and cutting fluids used to cool or lubricate metal during metalworking, is associated with higher odds of multiple sclerosis (MS), according to a study published in Neurology. The study does not prove that exposure to these lubricants causes MS. It only shows an association.

mix_items.title: Longer estrogen exposure linked to better brain vessel health in older women
mix_items.summary: Women who had a longer reproductive period and had used or are using hormone replacement therapy showed fewer signs of damage to the small blood vessels in the brain later in life. This is shown by a study led by researchers at Karolinska Institutet, published in the journal Neurology.

mix_items.title: Blood pressure medication and vibration may boost brain waste clearance
mix_items.summary: The brain's own clearance mechanisms are most active during sleep. Researchers have now shown that this natural clearance process can also be enhanced while people are awake. A novel vasomechanical treatment increased the removal of harmful proteins from participants' brains.

mix_items.title: AI starts writing acne prescriptions without a doctor's visit in one state
mix_items.summary: Utah has become the first state to let an artificial intelligence (AI) program prescribe medication without a doctor writing the prescription, starting with acne treatments.

mix_items.title: New CRISPR proteins expand editing access to heart disease genes
mix_items.summary: Rice University's Han Xiao has used his AI-supported Sequence Display technology to expand the targeting abilities of CRISPR/Cas9. In a paper recently published in Nature Communications, Xiao evolved several variants of a compact Cas9 that could efficiently target stretches of DNA previously inaccessible for editing. The research included a proof-of-concept study in which the evolved Cas9s were successfully used to edit two genes found in coronary heart disease.

mix_items.title: Key gene preserves lifelong supply of stem cells that make bone healing possible, study suggests
mix_items.summary: The action of a key gene is required to maintain a lifelong supply of stem cells that make bone healing possible, a new study finds.

mix_items.title: Rapid tau spread may explain why midlife Alzheimer's progresses more rapidly
mix_items.summary: Patients with early-onset Alzheimer's disease, whose symptoms start before age 65, have more extensive deposits of tau, a hallmark protein of the condition, compared with patients whose symptoms start at 65-plus, a new study found. What's more, tau accumulates at more than twice the rate in younger compared to older patients and spreads widely throughout the brain.

mix_items.title: Experimental ultrasound implant could help guide care after spinal cord injury
mix_items.summary: A team of engineers and surgeons from Johns Hopkins Medicine has published its first proof-of-concept study that shows temporarily implanting a tiny ultrasonic device into the location of a spinal cord injury can be feasible, safe and potentially useful. These findings, which mark an early midpoint in a multitiered research journey to develop and study how the device could be used in clinical care, were published in Science Advances.

mix_items.title: From green smoothies to stem‑cell supplements—online 'immune‑boosting' ideas may lead you astray
mix_items.summary: We all want a well-functioning immune system to help us fight invasive bacteria and viruses and recover faster from illness. Popular "immune-boosting" ideas, however, might be more of a hindrance than a help.

mix_items.title: Suriname’s rich archaeological history may hold keys to conservation
mix_items.summary: Suriname pledges to save its forests but neglects the ancient human history hidden within them, experts say.

mix_items.title: A town-wide ‘living laboratory’ shows how green spaces can combat climate extremes
mix_items.summary: Stoke Park is a natural haven in a busy British town. Centered in Guildford, Surrey, its rolling fields pop with wildflowers in the spring; birds sing and ducks paddle serenely in a pond beside ornamental gardens; and the sun casts dappled shade on the grass from oak, spruce and beech trees, scattered across 52 hectares […]

mix_items.title: Why I sent my archive of nature’s sounds to France (commentary)
mix_items.summary: It is a peculiar irony: as technology reaches ever deeper into Earth’s living systems, the primal sonic expressions of the natural world—wind, water, leaf, and creature—have never been more imperiled. Soundscape ecology rests on a simple conviction: the collective voices of the nonhuman world are not only eloquent, but essential. Recorded and preserved over time, […]

mix_items.title: US public lands tracker highlights the collective impact of Trump policies
mix_items.summary: In his second term as the U.S. president, Donald Trump has taken actions to remove protections from at least 34.8 million hectares (86 million acres) of public lands, according to the advocacy group Center for American Progress. The nonprofit Conservation Lands Foundation (CLF) recently catalogued 12 such policy actions in its newly released Public Lands […]

mix_items.title: Cyclone batters India’s eastern coast, killing 3 and damaging homes and farmland
mix_items.summary: KAKINADA, India (AP) — A powerful cyclone battered India ’s Andhra Pradesh state on Wednesday, killing at least three people and damaging homes and farmland after authorities evacuated tens of thousands of people, officials said. Cyclone Arnab made landfall early Wednesday as a very severe cyclonic storm before weakening to a severe cyclonic storm as […]

mix_items.title: Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has vanished in just five years
mix_items.summary: Switzerland’s glaciers are disappearing at an alarming rate, losing more than 5% of their ice volume in 2026 alone. Some of the country’s most famous glaciers experienced their worst melting on record, while several smaller glaciers vanished completely. Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has disappeared in just five years, driven by unusually snowless winters and extreme summer heat.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a surprising twist in Japan's 7,300-year-old volcanic apocalypse
mix_items.summary: A catastrophic volcanic eruption 7,300 years ago devastated Japan, but new research reveals that its impact on prehistoric populations was far more complex than previously believed. While some communities disappeared or declined, others unexpectedly flourished as survivors migrated, adapted, and found new ways to thrive.

mix_items.title: DNA recording system reveals how a single cell becomes a body
mix_items.summary: Scientists have traced the development of a mouse embryo from its first two cells to the formation of organs, using a remarkable DNA recording system that reveals the family history of individual cells. Their findings uncover how different cell types emerge on their own schedules and could help explain what goes wrong in birth defects, genetic disorders, and cancer.

mix_items.title: Europe's new Sentinel-3C satellite just sent back spectacular images of Earth
mix_items.summary: Europe's Sentinel-3C satellite has returned breathtaking images of Earth just two weeks after launch, revealing the snowy Alps, frozen Arctic islands, and brilliant turquoise Caribbean waters. Its first measurements also show promising results for tracking rising seas, melting ice sheets, and other changes reshaping our planet.

mix_items.title: Scientists uncover the 2.3-billion-year-old secret that helped keep Earth habitable
mix_items.summary: Scientists may have solved a 2.3-billion-year-old mystery about how Earth maintained enough oxygen to support life. Ancient rocks reveal that phosphorus recycling in the oceans created a self-sustaining cycle that helped keep oxygen levels high, even as the planet underwent dramatic environmental changes. The discovery challenges assumptions about Earth's early atmosphere and raises new questions about why complex life took so long to emerge.

mix_items.title: Scientists find a surprising genetic twist behind octopus intelligence
mix_items.summary: The remarkable intelligence of octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish may trace back to an ancient reshuffling of their DNA that created new connections between genes. Scientists discovered that these changes in the genome's 3D structure may have helped drive the evolution of their unusually complex nervous systems.
